items.title: Optional filters narrow access, they never widen it
items.body:
**Key: A and B; C matches Active but is outside what Acme may see.**

The question the endpoint answers is not "which contracts are Active?" but "which contracts that this caller may see are also Active?" Ownership is always part of the query. With the country parameter removed, Acme can receive A and B, and C stays excluded because it belongs to another company. Each optional filter can only take rows away from what ownership allows.

Why the others are wrong:
- **A, B and C**: a missing country filter does not remove the ownership rule; C fails it whatever filters are sent.
- **A only, via a PH default**: nothing substitutes a default country for an omitted parameter; B is a valid Acme contract.
- **A, B and D**: dropping the country filter leaves the state filter in place, so the Draft contract D still fails it.

excerpts.quote: Now remove the country parameter. Acme can receive A and B, but still not C.
Optional filters can narrow access; they cannot grant more of it.

items.title: API validation and database constraints do different jobs
items.body:
**Key: keep the check, as the EF annotation is no substitute for it on SQLite.**

Lesson 1 separates two responsibilities. API validation gives the caller a useful, field-specific error and refuses values outside the documented contract. Database constraints protect stored relationships and uniqueness, even when the writer is not this HTTP endpoint. A maximum-length annotation on the entity does not do the first job, especially with SQLite, so the trimmed-name check stays.

Why the others are wrong:
- **SQLite returns the same 400 itself**: the annotation is not a substitute for API validation; the database does not produce a field-specific 400.
- **Constraints already give field-specific errors**: constraints protect stored data; the friendly error is the API's job.
- **Run the check after saving**: validation happens before saving, and the test checks both the 400 and that the rejected row was never stored.

excerpts.quote: An EF maximum-length annotation is not a substitute for the first responsibility, especially with SQLite.
Database constraints protect stored relationships and uniqueness even when a writer is not this HTTP endpoint.

items.title: Start here: Atlas explained through its decision records
items.body:
Atlas is an employer-of-record backend: an ASP.NET Core minimal API over EF Core and SQLite that runs contracts, leave, expenses, payroll and invoicing for client companies. This pack is built from **docs/adr/**, the architecture decision records. Each ADR is short and has the same three parts: **Context** (the problem), **Decision** (what was chosen) and **Consequences** (what that costs and how it is tested).

A good reading order:

1. ADR 0002 and 0003: who the callers are and what each kind of key may see or do.
2. ADR 0004 and 0007: two persistence decisions forced by SQLite.
3. ADR 0005, 0006 and 0008: money, salary history and payroll runs.
4. ADR 0009: the shape of errors and of list responses.

Every ADR names the class that implements it. Open that class next to the ADR and check each claim against the code line by line.

excerpts.quote: Use **EF Core + SQLite** as the only persistence

readMore.why: The wider architecture tour: projects, request pipeline and the main domain areas.
The index of all eleven ADRs with one line on each.

items.title: Two version checks cover two different moments
items.body:
**Key: one catches staleness at load time, the other changes made after it.**

The early expected-version check compares the version the caller saw with the version just loaded. It gives a clear failure when the request is already stale. But another request can still change the row between that check and the save. EF's UPDATE includes the original Version in its WHERE clause, so if the row changed in that gap the update matches no row and EF reports a concurrency conflict. The lesson's point is that you need both because they act at different moments.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The early check is enough**: it cannot see a change that happens after it ran; the WHERE clause can.
- **The WHERE clause is enough**: it would catch the conflict, but the early check is what gives a clear failure for a request that was stale from the start.
- **A duplicate kept for safety**: the two checks are not the same test.

excerpts.quote: The database condition catches changes that happen after that check. You need both places because they operate at different moments.

items.title: ThenBy extends an order; a second OrderBy replaces it
items.body:
**Key: the Id order replaces the name order instead of breaking its ties.**

Names are not unique, so the list sorts by name and then by Id to give every row a definite position before paging. ThenBy adds a secondary key to the existing order. A second OrderBy starts a new order and replaces the first, so after the refactor the workers would come back sorted by Id alone and the name ordering would be lost.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Nothing changes**: only ThenBy appends; the lesson says a second OrderBy would replace the first order.
- **Tied names become unique**: the data does not change, and the lesson warns against making names unique to hide a query-design issue.
- **The query is refused**: the lesson describes the second OrderBy as replacing the order, not as an error.

excerpts.quote: `ThenBy` extends an order; a second `OrderBy` would replace the first order.

items.title: Convert the invoice total once, not each line
items.body:
**Key: once, to the summed invoice total, rounding that single product.**

PayrollAssessment sums the lines, adds the management fee, and only then converts: RoundMoney(total * fxRate.Value). ADR 0005 lists this rule: convert the already-summed total once, never per line. Converting and rounding each line could leave the converted total a cent away from the converted sum.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Per line, then sum**: this is the drift the ADR is written to avoid.
- **At payment time**: ADR 0008 applies the period's effective FX rate when the run is completed and the invoice issued; nothing re-converts at payment.
- **Never converted**: the assessment returns a TotalInBillingCurrency, and a missing FX rate makes completion fail with 409.

excerpts.quote: fxRate is null ? null : PayrollCalculator.RoundMoney(total * fxRate.Value));

items.title: Country.Version is where two different decisions meet
items.body:
**Key: creation also touches Country.Version, so the stale writer conflicts.**

Contract creation and the hiring pause write different records, so their own version tokens would never clash. To make them meet, creation and activation deliberately touch Country.Version when they save, and the pause changes that same country row. Whichever writer holds a stale country version gets a concurrency conflict. The lesson names the cost: unrelated hiring operations in one country can now conflict and need a reload, which it accepts for a simple, visible rule.

Why the others are wrong:
- **A lock held by the pause**: optimistic concurrency takes no lock; the conflict is detected at save time.
- **The pause deletes in-flight drafts**: nothing cancels other requests; the stale writer simply fails.
- **The contract's own Version detects it**: the pause does not change the contract row, so only the shared country row can reveal the conflict.

excerpts.quote: Creation and activation therefore touch Country.Version when saving.
unrelated hiring operations in one country may conflict and require a reload.

items.title: A prefix search treats % and _ as plain characters
items.body:
**Key: names starting with a literal `%_`, shown by a seeded `%_` name.**

The prefix query uses StartsWith instead of concatenating the caller's text into a LIKE pattern, so `%` and `_` keep their literal meaning. The tests seed names that begin with `%_` and prove the search returns that name rather than every name. A happy-path example such as `ac` would pass even if the characters were treated as wildcards, so it cannot catch this bug.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Every client name via LIKE wildcards**: that is the accidental behavior the seeded test exists to catch.
- **A 400 for non-letter characters**: the lesson defines `%` and `_` in a prefix as literal characters, not invalid input.
- **Accent-folded matches shown by `ac`**: the implementation makes no accent-folding promise, and the `ac` example alone would not catch wildcard behavior.

excerpts.quote: A prefix containing `%` or `_` means those literal characters.
This implementation does not promise accent folding or international linguistic search.

items.title: Core idea: two persistence decisions that SQLite forced
items.body:
SQLite is a small embedded database with very few column types. Two Atlas decisions exist because of that.

**Storing timestamps.** EF Core picks a column type for each .NET type. Read the Context of ADR 0004 to see what the default would have been for DateTimeOffset and why that is a problem for sorting and range filters. Then find the value converter in AtlasDbContext: a value converter is a pair of functions, one used when writing a property and one when reading it. Work out for yourself what information survives the round trip and what does not.

**Concurrent edits.** Two HTTP requests can load the same row, change it and save. Optimistic concurrency means no lock is taken; instead a column is compared at save time and a mismatch fails the save. In ADR 0007 and AtlasDbContext, look for three things: which entities take part, where the number is changed, and which class turns the failure into an HTTP response.

excerpts.quote: Entities whose updates can race use Version as an optimistic-concurrency

readMore.why: The concurrency-token loop, the SaveChanges overrides and the converter class.

items.title: Every request re-reads the key, so revocation is immediate
items.body:
**Key: on its next request, as every request looks up ApiUsers.**

HandleAuthenticateAsync runs SingleOrDefaultAsync on ApiUsers for the header value on every request and fails when the user is missing, inactive or expired. ADR 0002 counts this as a benefit: the one indexed lookup per request doubles as the revocation check.

Why the others are wrong:
- **When its JWT expires**: Atlas issues no JWTs; the ADR lists signing, refresh and clock skew as infrastructure it avoids.
- **After a key cache refreshes**: nothing caches keys; the handler queries the database each time.
- **Only once the row is deleted**: keys are revoked by deactivation, and rows are kept for the audit trail.

excerpts.quote: if (user is null || !user.IsActive || user.ExpiresAtUtc <= now)

items.title: The employee share is the remainder, never rounded on its own
items.body:
**Key: MonthlyCost - EmployerShare, so both shares re-add to the cent.**

BenefitPlan line 39 rounds the employer share once; line 42 defines EmployeeShare as MonthlyCost - EmployerShare. Because one side is the remainder of the other, employer plus employee always equals the premium exactly. ADR 0005 names this case explicitly.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Rounding (1 - rate) on its own**: rounding both sides independently can make the split one cent off the premium, which is the drift the ADR forbids.
- **Banker's rounding to offset bias**: Atlas has one rounding function and it uses AwayFromZero.
- **Truncating toward zero**: nothing in the money code truncates; RoundMoney rounds.

excerpts.quote: public decimal EmployeeShare => MonthlyCost - EmployerShare;

items.title: Check the original characters before normalizing them
items.body:
**Key: uppercasing can map a non-ASCII letter to ASCII and hide the violation.**

The promise is "three ASCII letters". Uppercasing is a normalization step, and in some cases it maps a non-ASCII character to an ASCII one. If the check ran on the uppercased text, an input that broke the promise could pass because the evidence was erased. So the ASCII check reads the original trimmed characters, and only accepted text is uppercased. The tests use a non-ASCII long-s example to exercise exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Lowercase like ` usd ` would be rejected**: the lesson shows ` usd ` is accepted and becomes `USD`.
- **A currency registry check**: the stories validate shape only; a fictional `XYZ` is accepted.
- **Digits like U1D would pass**: `U1D` fails shape validation either way; the reason given is the non-ASCII mapping.

excerpts.quote: Uppercasing first can map a non-ASCII character into an ASCII character in some cases.
A fictional `XYZ` is accepted because these stories validate shape, not membership in an external currency registry.

items.title: A stale Version becomes a 409, not a lost update
items.body:
**Key: a 409 ProblemDetails telling it to reload the resource and retry.**

Both callers loaded the same Version. The first save bumps it, so the second save's concurrency check matches no row and EF throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. DecideAsync does not catch it, so it reaches the global ConcurrencyExceptionHandler, which asks DatabaseConflicts.IsWriteConflict and writes a 409 with the detail "Reload it and retry".

Why the others are wrong:
- **A 200 that overwrites the first approval**: that lost update is exactly what the token prevents; the ADR says the winner's decision stands.
- **412 because no If-Match was sent**: Atlas does not use ETag preconditions; the ADR only mentions them as a possible later use.
- **A 500 because nothing maps the exception**: the registered IExceptionHandler maps it.

excerpts.quote: detail: "The resource was modified by another request. Reload it and retry."

items.title: Version tokens cannot see a race between two inserts
items.body:
**Key: neither insert updates a shared existing row whose version could clash.**

A version token works by putting the originally loaded version into an UPDATE's condition. Two new leave requests each insert their own new row. Neither updates an existing row the other also changed, so there is no version for either to find stale, and both reservations succeed against the same remaining balance. Learning note 08 lists what a real guarantee needs: a shared balance or version row, suitable transaction isolation, or another database-backed coordination policy.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Checked on approval only**: the reason is structural, not timing; the inserts share no row to compare.
- **SQLite serializes the inserts**: both requests read the balance before either inserted, so both saw five days.
- **A 409 like a stale write**: that path needs an existing row whose version changed; here there is none.

excerpts.quote: Their own version tokens cannot conflict because they update no shared existing row.

items.title: UTC ticks keep the instant and drop the offset
items.body:
**Key: the same instant, 02:00 with a zero offset; the +08:00 is gone.**

The converter writes value.UtcTicks and reads new DateTimeOffset(ticks, TimeSpan.Zero). 10:00 at +08:00 is 02:00 UTC, so the ticks describe 02:00 UTC and the value comes back as 02:00+00:00. ADR 0004 calls this out: the offset is discarded but the instant is the same, and a round-trip test documents it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **10:00 at +08:00**: there is no offset column; only one long is stored.
- **10:00 at a zero offset**: that would move the instant by eight hours; using UtcTicks prevents it.
- **Cut to whole seconds**: ticks keep 100 ns precision, and no string parsing is involved.

excerpts.quote: The original offset is discarded: a value written at `+08:00` reads back at offset zero.

items.title: A change effective mid-month owns the whole month
items.body:
**Key: the new salary for the whole of May, with no proration by day.**

EffectiveForMonth computes the month end (31 May), keeps records with EffectiveDate on or before it, orders by EffectiveDate then CreatedAtUtc, and takes the last one. The 15 May record qualifies and is the latest, so it is used for all of May. ADR 0006 records this as an accepted simplification.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Prorated by days**: the ADR says there is no intra-month proration for amendments.
- **Starts in the first full month**: the filter compares against the month's end, not its start.
- **Averaged**: LastOrDefault returns one record; nothing averages two.

excerpts.quote: var monthEnd = new DateOnly(year, month, 1).AddMonths(1).AddDays(-1);
a change effective mid-month owns that **whole** month (no intra-month proration).

items.title: Another client's resource looks exactly like a missing one
items.body:
**Key: 404, exactly as if that contract id did not exist at all.**

The contract GET loads by id and returns Results.NotFound() when the row is null OR when !user.CanViewClient(contract.ClientId). Both branches produce the same response, so a client key cannot learn that another client's id exists. ADR 0003 applies this to reads and writes.

Why the others are wrong:
- **403, role too weak**: 403 is for a caller who can see the resource but lacks the role; using it here would reveal that the contract exists.
- **401**: the key authenticated successfully; 401 is for a missing or unknown key.
- **200 with fields masked**: no data from another client is returned at all.

excerpts.quote: return contract is null || !user.CanViewClient(contract.ClientId)

items.title: Filter the population before you aggregate it
items.body:
**Key: the total and client breakdown still describe every country.**

A headcount report has several aggregates: an overall total, a country breakdown and a client breakdown. They must all describe the same population. If the report is computed over everyone and only the final country array is trimmed to PH, the country row looks right while the total and the client counts still include workers from other countries. ReportService avoids this by applying the filter before selecting and grouping, and the test checks the sum of client counts as well as the visible country rows.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Nothing, if the PH row is right**: the PH row being right is exactly what hides the misleading total.
- **Only the PH row is wrong**: the PH row is fine; the other aggregates are the problem.
- **Country rows missing, totals correct**: it is the reverse; the visible rows are trimmed and the totals are not.

excerpts.quote: Filtering the final country array alone would leave a misleading overall total and client breakdown.

items.title: An out-of-range page size is a validation error
items.body:
**Key: a 400 ValidationProblem with an error under the pageSize key.**

Pagination.Validate checks pageSize is < 1 or > MaxPageSize (200), adds errors["pageSize"], and returns Results.ValidationProblem(errors). The list endpoint returns that result before it touches the database. ADR 0009 states the same rule: default 50, max 200, out of range is 400.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Clamped to 200**: nothing clamps; the value is rejected.
- **All 500 rows**: the maximum is enforced, not advisory.
- **The default of 50**: the default is used only when pageSize is absent (pageSize ?? DefaultPageSize), not when it is invalid.

excerpts.quote: if (pageSize is < 1 or > MaxPageSize)

items.title: Core idea: money, rounding and which period a value belongs to
items.body:
Payroll adds and splits money many times, so a cent can appear or vanish if every step rounds on its own. ADR 0005 states one policy for this. As you read it, list each calculation it names (payroll amounts, benefit split, FX, final pay) and, for each one, which number is rounded and which numbers are derived from it by plain arithmetic. Then open PayrollCalculator.RoundMoney and note the midpoint rule it passes to Math.Round; look up the MidpointRounding enum if the options are new.

ADR 0006 and ADR 0008 are about time. Salary history is append-only: new terms are added as records with an effective date, never edited in place. ADR 0008 describes what creating a payroll run stores and what completing it does. Read SalaryRecord.EffectiveForMonth slowly and trace it by hand for a raise that starts in the middle of a month, and for an amendment that arrives after a run already exists.

excerpts.quote: Payroll is the heart of the product
Append-only salary history with effective-for-month selection

readMore.why: The single rounding function and the per-country payroll calculation.
How the record for a month is selected.

items.title: Each Where refines a description; nothing runs until materialization
items.body:
**Key: it makes a more specific query that runs only once materialized.**

An EF query built from Where calls is a description of database work. Adding the ownership Where and then the status and country Where calls just makes that description more specific. Only a database operation, such as the paging helper's count and page fetch, turns it into SQL and rows. That is also why the ownership rule is safe: it is part of the one query, not a check applied to rows already loaded.

Why the others are wrong:
- **It filters rows the previous Where already loaded**: no Where loads anything on its own.
- **One more SQL statement per Where, intersected in memory**: the conditions are combined into one description before anything executes.
- **Load every contract, then drop the foreign ones**: the lesson says explicitly that this is not what happens.

excerpts.quote: The query is a description until a database operation materializes it. Adding another Where builds a more specific description.

items.title: Prove one validation rule with an otherwise valid request
items.body:
**Key: otherwise valid, so the 400 can only come from the name rule.**

A 400 response says that some rule rejected the request, not which one. If the body has an invalid email, a missing country and an overlong name together, the test passes even when the name rule is broken, because one of the other rules still produces the 400. Keeping every unrelated field valid makes the name the only possible cause, so the test really proves the rule it is named after.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Several invalid fields at once**: this is the exact case the lesson warns about; the 400 no longer identifies the rule that worked.
- **Empty apart from the name**: missing required fields are other reasons for a 400.
- **Random values on each run**: random fields can be invalid too, and a boundary test needs a repeatable input.

excerpts.quote: a 400 response would not establish which rule worked. Keep unrelated fields valid when proving one rule.

items.title: Why TryParse alone cannot validate an enum filter
items.body:
**Key: it parses it, which is why the rule adds an Enum.IsDefined check.**

Enum.TryParse answers a narrow question: can this text be converted to the enum's underlying representation? `999` is a valid integer, so it converts, even though the enum declares only Draft, Active and Terminated. Parsing and checking the allowed set are different steps, so the shared defined-enum rule checks both, and also rejects comma-separated combinations because these filters take one value, not a flags expression. A name like `Active` or a defined number like `1` still works.

Why the others are wrong:
- **It returns false for 999**: the lesson says TryParse can successfully parse 999 for this enum.
- **Only with [Flags]**: the enum here has no flags role; TryParse still parses 999.
- **Maps to the nearest member**: nothing rounds a number to a declared label; undefined values are rejected by the IsDefined step.

excerpts.quote: It can successfully parse `999` even when the enum declares only Draft, Active, and Terminated.
The shared defined-enum rule checks parsing and Enum.IsDefined.

items.title: A created payroll run is a snapshot
items.body:
**Key: the snapshot from run creation; the amendment hits the next run.**

ADR 0008: creating a run computes and stores every Payslip immediately, and from then on the run is a snapshot that later amendments do not rewrite. Its Consequences section states the ordering case directly: an amendment approved after run creation affects the next run, and tests pin it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Draft runs recalculate on completion**: completing a run issues invoices; the ADR says there is no recalculate-draft operation.
- **New gross, old deductions**: payslips are computed together at creation; nothing mixes two sets of terms.
- **Locked until recalculated**: nothing blocks the run, and corrections would be a new feature, not a mutation.

excerpts.quote: an amendment approved after run creation affects the *next* run (pinned by tests)

items.title: RoundMoney uses AwayFromZero at two places
items.body:
**Key: 2.35, because a midpoint is rounded away from zero.**

RoundMoney is Math.Round(amount, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero). 2.345 sits exactly halfway between 2.34 and 2.35, and AwayFromZero picks 2.35. ADR 0005 chose this because it is predictable for people checking payslips by hand and matches statutory tables.

Why the others are wrong:
- **2.34, to the even digit**: that is MidpointRounding.ToEven, the default for Math.Round with no mode argument; Atlas passes AwayFromZero explicitly.
- **2.345, three places for FX**: RoundMoney always rounds to 2 places; FX results go through the same function.
- **2.34, truncated**: Math.Round rounds; it does not truncate.

excerpts.quote: Math.Round(amount, 2, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero);

items.title: A valid GUID with no match is an empty list, not an error
items.body:
**Key: an empty matching collection, with the GUID accepted as valid.**

Lesson 1 separates three cases that are easy to blur. A filter value that is a syntactically valid GUID is accepted even when no payroll run has that id; the query simply matches nothing, so the list is empty. Malformed GUID text is different: it fails binding. A detail route that looks up one document by id is different again: a missing document is a 404. None of these is a database crash.

Why the others are wrong:
- **A 404 like a detail route**: 404 belongs to a lookup of one missing resource, not to a list filter.
- **A binding error**: binding fails only for malformed GUID text; a well-formed GUID binds.
- **A database error from a foreign key lookup**: the lesson stresses these cases are not database crashes; the filter just matches no rows.

excerpts.quote: An invoice payrollRunId filter accepts a syntactically valid GUID even if no such run exists; it then returns an empty matching collection.

items.title: Two ANDed client filters match nothing
items.body:
**Key: 200 and an empty array: both client filters are applied together.**

For a non-admin, line 31 adds Where(c => c.ClientId == ownClientId). Line 33 then adds Where(c => c.ClientId == clientId) whenever the query string has one. EF combines the two Where calls with AND, and no contract has two client ids, so the page is empty (X-Total-Count is 0). Note the gap: ADR 0003 and the comment on line 29 say lists are scoped "whatever filter they pass", which reads as if the filter were ignored. The code applies it.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Own contracts, filter ignored**: that is the comment's reading, not what lines 33-36 do.
- **404 / 403**: list endpoints never refuse by ownership; they scope the query.

excerpts.quote: query = query.Where(c => c.ClientId == clientId);

items.title: Visible but not permitted is a 403
items.body:
**Key: 403, since it can see the request but lacks the role to act.**

LeaveEndpoints.DecideAsync first returns 404 if the request is missing or belongs to another client (CanViewClient). A viewer of its own client passes that check. Next, CanManageClient fails for a viewer, and the endpoint returns a 403 problem saying only platform admins or the client's own admins can decide leave requests.

Why the others are wrong:
- **404**: hiding existence is for other clients' data; this request belongs to the viewer's own client, which it may read.
- **409**: that is a domain-state conflict, raised only after the role check passes.
- **401**: the key is valid, so authentication succeeded.

excerpts.quote: if (!user.CanManageClient(request.Contract!.ClientId))

items.title: Omitted, true and false are three different filter inputs
items.body:
**Key: isActive=false, which then skips the filter and returns every country.**

A nullable Boolean carries three inputs: omitted means do not filter, true means active countries, false means inactive countries. A condition that runs only when the value is true never runs for false, so a request for inactive countries gets the unfiltered list, exactly like an omitted value. The implementation instead checks whether a value was supplied and then compares to that value. The `currencyCode=USD&isActive=false` test proves both filters stay active, even though its expected result is empty.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Omitted returns only active countries**: with this bug, omitted still applies no filter, which is its correct meaning.
- **true also returns inactive ones**: true is the one case the buggy condition handles.
- **A nullable Boolean has two meaningful values**: the lesson's table lists three.

excerpts.quote: A condition that runs only when the value is true loses the false case.

items.title: Text timestamps cannot be compared as instants
items.body:
**Key: the default is TEXT, which SQLite cannot compare as instants.**

ADR 0004's Context: SQLite has no native date-time type, EF Core's default stores DateTimeOffset as TEXT, and ORDER BY or range filters on those strings get the wrong SQL semantics or fall back to client-side evaluation. Integer ticks sort and compare correctly in SQL, which DateTimeOffsetConverterTests check.

Why the others are wrong:
- **EnsureCreated would fail**: a TEXT column is created without complaint; the problem only shows up in queries.
- **Disk space**: the ADR never mentions size; its concern is ordering and comparison.
- **Two servers disagree on local time**: the problem is how instants compare, not which zone a server uses.

excerpts.quote: SQLite cannot order or compare those strings as instants

items.title: Validate the whole batch before changing any item
items.body:
**Key: neither item, as every item is checked before any box is ticked.**

The batch endpoint works in two phases. First it checks the entire request: permission, item count, duplicate IDs, note lengths, that every item belongs to this contract, expected versions and completion state. Only after all of that passes does it change the validated items and save them together in one SaveChangesAsync. An item from another contract fails the membership check in phase one, so nothing is completed.

Why the others are wrong:
- **The first item, saved in turn**: a validate-and-save-per-item loop is the design the lesson warns against, because it leaves the first item complete when the second fails.
- **The first item, with the second listed as rejected**: there is no partial result; the request either commits as a set or not at all.
- **Both items, membership checked after saving**: membership is checked before anything changes.

excerpts.quote: inspect every item before checking any box. Once all checks pass, submit the set as one database operation.
A loop that validates and saves one item at a time can leave the first item complete when the second one fails.

items.title: The DbContext bumps Version, so no endpoint can forget
items.body:
**Key: in AtlasDbContext, which bumps it for each Modified versioned entry.**

Both SaveChanges overrides call BumpVersions before the base save. BumpVersions walks `ChangeTracker.Entries<IVersioned>()` and runs `entry.Entity.Version++` for every entry whose state is Modified. OnModelCreating registers the same property as a concurrency token, so EF puts the old value in the UPDATE's WHERE clause.

Why the others are wrong:
- **A SQLite rowversion column**: ADR 0007 says SQLite has no rowversion type; that is why the token is application-managed.
- **Each endpoint adds one**: the ADR's reason for centralising the bump is that no endpoint can forget it.
- **A trigger from EnsureCreated**: no trigger is defined anywhere; the increment is plain C#.

excerpts.quote: if (entry.State == EntityState.Modified)
centralizing the bump in `SaveChanges` means no endpoint can forget it.

items.title: Core idea: keys, roles and how lists are bounded
items.body:
Atlas has no login page. Callers send a static key in a header, and ApiKeyAuthenticationHandler turns it into a principal with a role and, for client roles, one client id. Read ADR 0002 for the trade-offs of that choice compared with signed tokens, and read the handler to see what it checks on each request.

ADR 0003 then defines two different refusal status codes and when each applies. Build a small table with rows for read, write and list, and columns for own client and other client, and fill each cell from the ADR. Then check the cells against AuthorizationExtensions and two endpoint files, ContractEndpoints and LeaveEndpoints.

Header-based pagination in about fifty lines.

items.title: Page metadata travels in headers
items.body:
**Key: in the X-Total-Count, X-Page and X-Page-Size response headers.**

ToPageAsync counts the query, writes those three headers on the response, and returns a plain `List<T>`. ADR 0009 chose this so that clients already parsing a JSON array kept working when pagination arrived.

Why the others are wrong:
- **An { items, total } envelope**: the ADR names this option and rejects it to avoid a breaking change.
- **A Link header with rel=next**: no Link header is written anywhere in Pagination.cs.
- **A metadata object appended to the array**: the body holds only the page's items.

excerpts.quote: http.Response.Headers["X-Total-Count"] = total.ToString();

items.title: A template is configuration; checklist rows are copied work
items.body:
**Key: it keeps yesterday's title, and only later contracts get the new one.**

When a contract is created, its checklist rows are built from the country template with `new OnboardingItem`: new IDs and independent state. From then on the rows belong to that contract's onboarding, not to the template. Editing the template changes what future contracts receive; it does not rewrite work that already exists, so yesterday's contract keeps "Identity check".

Why the others are wrong:
- **Rows point at the template item**: template item IDs are not reused; the lesson says that would collapse two responsibilities into one record.
- **Renamed once the header version is bumped**: the template version describes the template; it does not push changes into existing checklists.
- **Dropped and rebuilt on the next read**: nothing re-applies the template to an existing contract.

excerpts.quote: A contract created yesterday keeps yesterday's title. A contract created tomorrow receives the new title.
